main.title: Emancipation Proclamation
main.summary: The Emancipation Proclamation, officially Proclamation 95, was a presidential proclamation and executive order issued by United States president Abraham Lincoln on January 1, 1863, during the American Civil War.

cards.heading: Emancipation Proclamation
cards.text:
The Emancipation Proclamation, officially Proclamation 95, was a presidential proclamation and executive order issued by United States president Abraham Lincoln on January 1, 1863, during the American Civil War. The Proclamation changed the legal status of more than 3.5 million enslaved African Americans in the secessionist Confederate states from enslaved to free. As soon as slaves escaped the control of their enslavers, either by fleeing to Union lines or through the advance of federal troops, they were permanently free. In addition, the Proclamation allowed for former slaves to "be received into the armed service of the United States". The Emancipation Proclamation played a significant part in the end of slavery in the United States.

On September 22, 1862, Lincoln issued the Preliminary Emancipation Proclamation (Proclamation 93).

main.title: London Underground
main.summary: The Metropolitan Railway opened in London on 10 January 1863 as the world's first underground passenger railway.

cards.heading: London Underground
cards.text: The Metropolitan Railway opened in London on 10 January 1863 as the world's first underground passenger railway. Its early lines were built by digging trenches and covering them again, placing trains beneath streets rather than adding more traffic to them. Later construction reached deeper circular tunnels, giving the network its Tube nickname. The City and South London Railway introduced underground electric traction in 1890. These successive approaches grew into a transport system serving London and neighbouring counties, with both underground routes and extensive surface sections.

main.title: Football begins to share one code
main.subtitle: The Football Association and common rules
main.summary: The Football Association was formed in London on 26 October 1863 to establish a common set of football rules.

cards.heading: The Football Association and common rules
cards.text: Representatives of London and suburban football clubs met at the Freemasons' Tavern on October 26, 1863, to form the Football Association. Clubs and schools played different versions of football, making a common code necessary for matches between them. Ebenezer Morley helped organise the meetings, which continued through the autumn as the Association settled its laws. Decisions over carrying the ball and hacking opponents' legs separated association football from other versions of the game and gave participating clubs a shared framework.

main.title: First International
main.summary: Workers meeting at St Martin's Hall in London founded the International Workingmen's Association in 1864.

cards.heading: First International
cards.text: Workers meeting at St Martin's Hall in London founded the International Workingmen's Association in 1864. Known as the First International, it sought to connect labour organisations and political groups across borders. Its first congress met in Geneva in 1866. Cooperation also brought disagreements about how socialism should be achieved: Marxists, followers of Proudhon and Bakunin's anarchist collectivists disputed the role of the state and political action. The Paris Commune of 1871 gave the organisation a major cause to defend, including through Marx's address The Civil War in France.

main.title: Maxwell publishes his electromagnetic theory
main.summary: James Clerk Maxwell published his electromagnetic theory in 1865, following its presentation in 1864. His equations connected electricity and magnetism and supplied a mathematical foundation for understanding light.

cards.heading: Maxwell publishes his electromagnetic theory
cards.text:
James Clerk Maxwell published his electromagnetic theory in 1865, following its presentation in 1864. His equations connected electricity and magnetism and supplied a mathematical foundation for understanding light.

Maxwell's equations are a set of coupled partial differential equations that describe how electric and magnetic fields are generated by electric charges and currents. Together with the Lorentz force law, they form the foundation of classical electromagnetism, classical optics, electric and magnetic circuits. The equations provide a mathematical model for electric, optical, and radio technologies, such as power generation, electric motors, wireless communication, lenses, and radar.

The microscopic equations have universal applicability but are unwieldy for common calculations. They relate the electric and magnetic fields to total charge and total current, including the complicated charges and currents in materials at the atomic scale.

main.title: Dynamite
main.summary: Dynamite is an explosive made of nitroglycerin, sorbents (such as powdered shells or clay), and stabilizers.

cards.heading: Dynamite
cards.text:
Dynamite is an explosive made of nitroglycerin, sorbents (such as powdered shells or clay), and stabilizers. It was invented by Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel in 1866 and patented the following year.

Dynamite was the first safely manageable explosive stronger than traditional black powder–based explosives and was widely adopted as a safer and more robust alternative shortly after its introduction. It allows the use of nitroglycerin's favorable explosive properties while greatly reducing its risk of accidental detonation.

main.title: The Sholes and Glidden typewriter takes shape
main.summary: Christopher Latham Sholes and Carlos Glidden developed their typewriter prototype in 1867. Pressing its keys made characters on paper mechanically; commercial typewriters followed in 1874.

cards.heading: The Sholes and Glidden typewriter takes shape
cards.text:
Christopher Latham Sholes and Carlos Glidden developed their typewriter prototype in 1867. Pressing its keys made characters on paper mechanically; commercial typewriters followed in 1874.

A typewriter is a mechanical or electromechanical machine for typing characters. Typically, a typewriter has an array of keys, and each one causes a different single character to be produced on paper by striking an inked ribbon selectively against the paper with a type element. Thereby, the machine produces a legible written document composed of ink and paper. By the end of the 19th century, a person who used such a device was also referred to as a typist or a typewriter.

The first commercial typewriters were introduced in 1874, but did not become common in offices in the United States until after the mid-1880s. The typewriter quickly became an indispensable tool for practically all writing other than personal handwritten correspondence. It was widely used by professional writers, in offices, in business correspondence in private homes, and by students preparing written assignments.

main.title: Mendeleev's periodic table
main.summary: Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic classification of the elements in 1869. Grouping elements by recurring properties made the table a practical way to understand relationships between substances.

cards.heading: Mendeleev's periodic table
cards.text:
Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic classification of the elements in 1869. Grouping elements by recurring properties made the table a practical way to understand relationships between substances.

The periodic table, also known as the periodic table of the elements, is an ordered arrangement of the chemical elements into rows ("periods") and columns ("groups"). An icon of chemistry, the periodic table is also widely used in physics and other sciences. It is a depiction of the periodic law, which states that when the elements are arranged in order of their atomic numbers an approximate recurrence of their properties is evident. The table is divided into four roughly rectangular areas called blocks. Elements in the same group tend to show similar chemical characteristics.

Vertical, horizontal and diagonal trends characterize the periodic table. Metallic character increases going down a group and from right to left across a period. Nonmetallic character increases going from the bottom left of the periodic table to the top right.

main.title: Rutgers and Princeton play collegiate football
main.subtitle: A starting point, before the modern gridiron game
main.summary: Rutgers beat Princeton on 6 November 1869 in a collegiate football match whose rules were closer to association football than today's American football.

cards.heading: A starting point, before the modern gridiron game
cards.text: Rutgers defeated Princeton by six goals to four in New Brunswick, New Jersey, on November 6, 1869. Traditionally recognised as the beginning of intercollegiate American football, the match fielded twenty-five players per side under rules drawn from London's Football Association code. Players kicked or batted the ball. Later developments, including Walter Camp's reforms, introduced eleven-player teams, the line of scrimmage and the system of downs that would define the gridiron game.

main.title: Suez Canal
main.summary: The Suez Canal opened on 17 November 1869 after a decade of construction.

cards.heading: Suez Canal
cards.text: The Suez Canal opened on 17 November 1869 after a decade of construction. Crossing Egypt's isthmus, it connected the Mediterranean and Red seas at sea level and gave ships a direct route between the North Atlantic and northern Indian Ocean. Vessels could avoid the much longer passage around southern Africa, changing the geography of trade between Europe and Asia. Ferdinand de Lesseps had established the Compagnie de Suez in 1858 to build it. The waterway runs between Port Said in the north and Suez in the south.
